Can a docker container be frozen and started quickly from a snapshot with processes already running?

Yes—on Linux, you can “freeze” a container and later “start” it again with the processes continuing from where they left off, using checkpoint/restore (typically via CRIU). CRIU+1

How it works (conceptually)

  • Checkpoint: dump process state (memory, registers, open FDs, etc.) to files on disk.

  • Restore: re-create the processes and resume execution from that state. CRIU

Docker: supported, but “experimental”

Docker has a docker checkpoint command set described as an experimental feature for checkpoint/restore. Docker Documentation
Typical shape:

  • docker checkpoint create <container> <name>

  • docker start --checkpoint <name> <container>

(Exact flags and availability depend on your engine/runtime setup, and CRIU must be available/compatible.)

Practical reality: it’s not as magical as a VM snapshot

Checkpoint/restore can be fast-ish, but it’s not always “instant”:

  • Restore time often scales with memory size and state complexity (writing/reading dumps).

  • Some things are hard or impossible to restore cleanly (see below).

If your main goal is “resume in a second with everything intact,” a VM suspend/resume snapshot often behaves closer to that expectation than container C/R.

Common limitations / gotchas

Checkpoint/restore is powerful but finicky:

  • Linux-only in practice (because it relies on Linux kernel features). CRIU is a Linux project. CRIU
    On macOS/Windows Docker Desktop, containers run inside a Linux VM, and C/R support may be limited by that environment.

  • Kernel / environment sensitivity: restore usually expects a very similar kernel + userspace + container config.

  • External resources can break restore: network connections, special devices, FUSE mounts, some IPC patterns, GPUs, etc. (CRIU is improving here, but this is the typical pain point).

  • Rootless vs root: tooling support varies (e.g., Podman’s CRIU integration notes root-only support in some setups). CRIU

If you’re actually trying to do this “for real”

Two mainstream routes:

  • Docker checkpoint/restore (experimental) using CRIU underneath. Docker Documentation

  • Podman checkpoint/restore (often considered the smoother path for C/R in practice, depending on distro/runtime). CRIU

And if you’re in Kubernetes land: container checkpointing exists and has been progressing (alpha → beta per CRIU’s K8s overview), and there’s even a dedicated working group as of Jan 2026. CRIU+1

If you tell me your platform (native Linux vs Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows) and whether you need “fast restart” vs “live migration / stateful resume”, I can point you to the least-painful approach for that specific goal.

Can I do it with apple/container?

Probably not in the way you mean (process checkpoint/restore).

Apple’s container runs each container inside a lightweight Linux VM on macOS. Apple Open Source That project definitely uses the word “snapshots”, but from the public issues/logging it’s referring to storage/image/rootfs snapshotting (e.g., rootfs.ext4 copies and large sparse snapshot files under ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.container/snapshots)—not “resume with processes already running.” GitHub+1

Also, the documented CLI surface (command categories and examples) doesn’t expose anything like checkpoint/restore or suspend/resume for live processes. Trunktail

What you can do instead (pragmatic options)

  • If you want fast startup: keep images warm/unpacked and avoid heavy init (the “snapshot” machinery here helps with image/rootfs management, not process state). GitHub+1

  • If you truly need “resume with processes”: use CRIU-based checkpoint/restore on native Linux runtimes that support it (Docker/Podman on Linux). CRIU is the standard mechanism for that feature. CRIU

  • On macOS specifically: the closest analog is usually VM suspend/resume (snapshot the VM), but Apple/container does not appear to expose that as a supported workflow via its CLI/docs today. Trunktail+1

If you tell me whether your goal is (A) “restart quickly” or (B) “resume exact process state”, I’ll suggest the simplest setup that actually works on macOS.
